Sen. Hicks’ study highlights need for improved safety in supervised visitation cases
Senator Carri Hicks says her interim study found gaps between policy and practice regarding child safety during court-ordered supervised visitations in Oklahoma. Following a tragic incident involving six-year-old Lizzy Feaster, Hicks outlined key areas needing reform and plans new legislation named 'Lizzy’s Law' for 2027.
Sen. Carri Hicks, D-Oklahoma City, said on Oct. 1 that her recent interim study on supervised visitation revealed a need to improve safety measures for children involved in court-ordered supervised visits and to increase accountability among those responsible for these processes.
Hicks initiated the study following the murder of six-year-old Lizzy Feaster by her father during a supervised visit in 2025, after which the father took his own life. The incident prompted an examination of current practices and standards related to supervised visitation across Oklahoma.
“We looked at the different kinds of supervised visitation, including children in the custody of the Department of Human Services, as well as children whose parents are separated or divorced. We know we’re not starting from scratch – there are policies and statutes that address how this is supposed to work in both circumstances,” Hicks said. “But this study underscored the fact that having standards in statute is not the same as having consistent standards in practice. First and foremost, safety must be the foundation.”
Based on testimony presented before the Senate’s Judiciary Committee during her study, Hicks identified several areas requiring further review: statewide minimum standards for providers; consistent training and background screening; clear protocols for high-risk cases; documentation and reporting requirements; procedures for violations or unsafe visits; oversight mechanisms; consideration of domestic violence dynamics; rural access issues; affordability concerns; sustainable funding models; and ways to evaluate system effectiveness.
“When a court orders supervised visitation, that order carries an expectation of safety. A child should not have to bear the consequences when the systems designed to protect them fail to communicate, fail to document, fail to train, or fail to act,” Hicks said. She announced plans to continue working on these issues throughout the interim period, and intends to introduce legislation called the Supervised Visitation Safety and Accountability Act—‘Lizzy’s Law’—for consideration during Oklahoma's 2027 legislative session.
